title: Light - Reflection and Refraction
subject: Science

items: Reflection of light is the phenomenon in which light bounces back into the same medium after falling on a surface.
The surface on which light falls is called the reflecting surface.
The ray of light that falls on the surface is called the incident ray.
The ray of light that bounces back is called the reflected ray.
The perpendicular line drawn to the reflecting surface at the point where light falls is called the normal.

blocks.text: There are two laws of reflection:

items: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection: \(\angle i = \angle r\).
The incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane.
Reflection can occur from different surfaces.
A smooth and polished surface gives regular reflection, while a rough surface gives irregular reflection.

blocks.text: A spherical mirror is a mirror whose reflecting surface is a part of a hollow sphere. There are two types of spherical mirrors:

items: Concave mirror – its reflecting surface is curved inwards.
Convex mirror – its reflecting surface is curved outwards.
Pole (\(P\)): The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.
Centre of curvature (\(C\)): The centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part.
Radius of curvature (\(R\)): The distance between the pole and the centre of curvature.
Principal axis: The straight line passing through the pole (\(P\)) and centre of curvature (\(C\)).
Principal focus (\(F\)): The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the principal axis meet or appear to meet after reflection.
Focal length (\(f\)): The distance between the pole and the principal focus.
When light rays coming from an object fall on a spherical mirror and are reflected, they may meet at a point or appear to meet at a point.
The image formed at this point is called the image of the object.

blocks.text: There are two types of images formed by spherical mirrors:

items: Real image: Formed when reflected light rays actually meet; it can be obtained on a screen; it is generally inverted.
Virtual image: Formed when reflected light rays appear to meet but do not actually meet; it cannot be obtained on a screen; it is generally erect.

blocks.text: Image Formation by a Concave Mirror
A concave mirror can form real or virtual images, depending on the position of the object. The position of the object can be:

items: Beyond \(C\)
At \(C\)
Between \(C\) and \(F\)
At \(F\)
Between \(F\) and \(P\)

blocks.text: The size and position of the image change according to the position of the object.
Image Formation by a Convex Mirror

items: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.
The image is formed behind the mirror, between \(P\) and \(F\).

notes.heading: 9.2.2 Representation of Images Formed by Spherical Mirrors Using Ray Diagrams

items: Ray diagrams are used to find the position, size and nature of an image formed by a spherical mirror.
We use some important rays whose paths after reflection are known.

blocks.text: Important Rays for a Concave Mirror

items: A ray parallel to the principal axis is reflected through the principal focus \(F\).
A ray passing through the principal focus \(F\) is reflected parallel to the principal axis.
A ray passing through the centre of curvature \(C\) is reflected back along the same path.
A ray striking the pole \(P\) is reflected according to the laws of reflection.

blocks.text: Important Ray for a Convex Mirror

items: A ray parallel to the principal axis is reflected in such a way that it appears to come from the principal focus \(F\) behind the mirror.
To locate an image, we usually draw at least two reflected rays. The point where the rays meet, or appear to meet, gives the position of the image.

notes.heading: 9.2.3 Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors

items: NCERT uses the New Cartesian Sign Convention for spherical mirrors.
The pole \(P\) of the mirror is taken as the origin.
The principal axis is taken as the \(x\)-axis.
All distances are measured from the pole \(P\).
Distances measured in the direction of incident light are taken as positive.
Distances measured in the opposite direction of incident light are taken as negative.
Heights measured above the principal axis are positive.
Heights measured below the principal axis are negative.

blocks.text: Since the object is usually placed in front of the mirror:
The focus and centre of curvature are also in front of the mirror:
The focus and centre of curvature are behind the mirror:
The sign convention helps us use the mirror formula correctly in numerical problems.
The relationship between the object distance \(u\), image distance \(v\) and focal length \(f\) of a spherical mirror is called the mirror formula:

items: \(u\) = object distance from the pole
\(v\) = image distance from the pole
\(f\) = focal length of the mirror

blocks.text: Magnification tells us how large or small the image is compared with the object. It is represented by \(m\):

items: \(h_i\) = height of the image
\(h_o\) = height of the object
\(v\) = image distance
\(u\) = object distance
If \(|m| > 1\), the image is larger than the object.
If \(|m| < 1\), the image is smaller than the object.
If \(|m| = 1\), the image is the same size as the object.
A positive \(m\) indicates an erect image.
A negative \(m\) indicates an inverted image.
Refraction of light is the change in the direction of light when it passes from one transparent medium to another.
Refraction occurs because the speed of light changes when it enters a different medium.
For example, when light travels from air to glass, its speed decreases and its direction changes.
When light travels from a rarer medium to a denser medium, it bends towards the normal.
When light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal.
If light falls normally on the surface, it does not change its direction, although its speed changes.

blocks.text: Example: A pencil partly immersed in water appears bent due to refraction of light.

notes.heading: 9.3.1 Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab

items: When a ray of light passes through a rectangular glass slab, it undergoes refraction at both surfaces of the slab.
When light travels from air to glass, it bends towards the normal because glass is optically denser than air.
When light travels from glass to air, it bends away from the normal.
The ray coming out of the glass slab is called the emergent ray.
The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, but it is shifted sideways.
This sideways shift is called lateral displacement.

blocks.text: The amount of lateral displacement depends on:

items: Thickness of the glass slab
Angle of incidence
Refractive index of the glass

blocks.text: Although the light ray changes direction inside the glass slab, the emergent ray remains parallel to the incident ray.

items: The refractive index of a medium tells us how much the speed of light changes when it enters that medium.
It is represented by the symbol \(\mu\) (mu).
\(c\) = speed of light in vacuum
\(v\) = speed of light in the given medium
The refractive index has no unit because it is a ratio of two speeds.
A medium with a higher refractive index is called optically denser.
A medium with a lower refractive index is called optically rarer.

blocks.text: Therefore, glass is optically denser than air.
Where \(i\) = angle of incidence and \(r\) = angle of refraction. Thus, refractive index helps us understand how strongly a medium bends light.

items: A lens is a transparent material, usually made of glass or plastic, bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which is curved.
A spherical lens has surfaces that are part of a sphere.
There are two main types of spherical lenses:
A convex lens is thicker at the centre and thinner at the edges.
It converges parallel rays of light.
Therefore, it is also called a converging lens.
A concave lens is thinner at the centre and thicker at the edges.
It diverges parallel rays of light.
Therefore, it is also called a diverging lens.
Optical centre (\(O\)): The central point of a lens through which a ray of light passes without changing its direction significantly.
Principal axis: The straight line passing through the optical centre and the centres of curvature of the lens surfaces.
Principal focus (\(F\)): The point on the principal axis where parallel rays meet or appear to meet after refraction.
Focal length (\(f\)): The distance between the optical centre \(O\) and the principal focus \(F\).
When light rays from an object pass through a spherical lens, they are refracted and may meet at a point or appear to meet at a point.
The point where the rays meet, or appear to meet, is called the image.

blocks.text: A convex lens can form real or virtual images, depending on the position of the object:

items: When the object is placed beyond the focal point, a real and inverted image is generally formed.
When the object is placed between the optical centre \(O\) and the focus \(F\), a virtual, erect and magnified image is formed.
A virtual image
An erect image
A diminished image

blocks.text: The image is formed between the optical centre \(O\) and the principal focus \(F\) on the same side of the lens as the object.

notes.heading: 9.3.5 Representation of Image Formation in Lenses Using Ray Diagrams

blocks.text: Ray diagrams are used to find the position, size and nature of the image formed by a lens.
Important Rays for a Convex Lens

items: A ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the principal focus \(F\) after refraction.
A ray passing through the principal focus \(F\) emerges parallel to the principal axis.
A ray passing through the optical centre \(O\) passes through the lens without changing its direction.

blocks.text: Important Rays for a Concave Lens

items: A ray parallel to the principal axis appears to come from the principal focus \(F\) after refraction.
A ray directed towards the principal focus \(F\) emerges parallel to the principal axis.
A ray passing through the optical centre \(O\) passes through the lens without changing its direction.
To locate the image, we usually draw two rays from the object.
The point where the refracted rays meet, or appear to meet, gives the position of the image.
The optical centre \(O\) of the lens is taken as the origin.
The principal axis is taken as the \(x\)-axis.
All distances are measured from the optical centre \(O\).
Distances measured in the direction of incident light are taken as positive.
Distances measured in the opposite direction of incident light are taken as negative.
Heights measured above the principal axis are positive.
Heights measured below the principal axis are negative.

The sign convention is important for using the lens formula and solving numerical problems.
The relationship between the object distance \(u\), image distance \(v\) and focal length \(f\) of a spherical lens is called the lens formula:

items: \(u\) = object distance from the optical centre
\(v\) = image distance from the optical centre
\(f\) = focal length of the lens

blocks.text: Magnification tells us how large or small the image is compared with the object. It is represented by \(m\):

items: \(h_i\) = height of the image
\(h_o\) = height of the object
\(v\) = image distance
\(u\) = object distance
If \(|m| > 1\), the image is larger than the object.
If \(|m| < 1\), the image is smaller than the object.
If \(|m| = 1\), the image is the same size as the object.
Positive \(m\) → image is erect.
Negative \(m\) → image is inverted.
The power of a lens tells us the ability of a lens to converge or diverge light.
It is represented by the symbol \(P\).
Here, \(f\) is the focal length of the lens in metres.
The SI unit of power is dioptre (D).
Convex lens has positive focal length, so its power is positive: \(\boxed{P > 0}\).
Concave lens has negative focal length, so its power is negative: \(\boxed{P < 0}\).

summary: Light reflects from surfaces obeying the two laws of reflection (∠i = ∠r, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane). Spherical mirrors are either concave (converging, f < 0) or convex (diverging, f > 0), with focal length f = R/2, governed by the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u and magnification m = h_i/h_o = -v/u under the New Cartesian Sign Convention. Refraction is the bending of light when passing from one transparent medium to another due to a change in speed, governed by Snell's law (sin i / sin r = μ = c/v). A rectangular glass slab shifts light laterally while keeping the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray. Spherical lenses — convex (converging, f > 0, P > 0) and concave (diverging, f < 0, P < 0) — form images described by the lens formula 1/f = 1/v - 1/u, magnification m = h_i/h_o = v/u, and lens power P = 1/f (in dioptres, where f is in metres).

qa.q: State the two laws of reflection of light.
qa.a: (1) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r). (2) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

qa.q: Define pole, centre of curvature, principal focus and focal length of a spherical mirror, and state the relation between R and f.
qa.a: The pole (P) is the centre of the reflecting surface; the centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the hollow sphere of which the mirror is a part; the principal focus (F) is the point on the principal axis where parallel rays meet or appear to meet after reflection; and the focal length (f = PF) is half the radius of curvature (f = R/2).

qa.q: Differentiate between real and virtual images, and state the nature of the image formed by a convex mirror.
qa.a: A real image forms when reflected rays actually meet, can be obtained on a screen, and is inverted. A virtual image forms when rays only appear to meet, cannot be obtained on a screen, and is erect. A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image behind the mirror between P and F.

qa.q: State the four standard rays used to draw ray diagrams for image formation by a concave mirror.
qa.a: (1) A ray parallel to the principal axis reflects through the focus F. (2) A ray passing through F reflects parallel to the principal axis. (3) A ray passing through the centre of curvature C reflects back along the same path. (4) A ray striking the pole P reflects such that ∠i = ∠r.
qa.section: 9.2.2 Representation of Images Formed by Spherical Mirrors Using Ray Diagrams

qa.q: According to the New Cartesian Sign Convention, what are the signs of u, f and R for a concave mirror and a convex mirror?
qa.a: Distances are measured from the pole P. Since the object is placed in front of the mirror, u < 0. For a concave mirror, the focus and centre of curvature lie in front of the mirror, so f < 0 and R < 0. For a convex mirror, they lie behind the mirror, so f > 0 and R > 0.
qa.section: 9.2.3 Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors

qa.q: Write the mirror formula and the magnification formula for a spherical mirror, and explain what the sign and magnitude of m indicate.
qa.a: Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. Magnification: m = h_i / h_o = -v / u. If |m| > 1 the image is magnified, if |m| < 1 it is diminished, and if |m| = 1 it is the same size. A positive m means a virtual, erect image; a negative m means a real, inverted image.

qa.q: Why does a ray of light bend when it travels obliquely from one transparent medium to another?
qa.a: Refraction occurs because the speed of light changes from one medium to another. Light bends towards the normal when going from an optically rarer to a denser medium, and away from the normal when going from a denser to a rarer medium.

qa.q: What is lateral displacement in a rectangular glass slab, and on what factors does it depend?
qa.a: When light passes through a rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways; this sideways shift is called lateral displacement. It depends on the thickness of the glass slab, the angle of incidence and the refractive index of the glass.
qa.section: 9.3.1 Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab

qa.q: Define the refractive index of a medium in terms of the speed of light and state Snell's law.
qa.a: The refractive index (μ) of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (c) to the speed of light in that medium (v): μ = c/v. By Snell's law, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant: sin i / sin r = μ.

qa.q: Distinguish between a convex lens and a concave lens.
qa.a: A convex lens is thicker at the centre than at the edges and converges parallel light rays (converging lens). A concave lens is thinner at the centre than at the edges and diverges parallel light rays (diverging lens).

qa.q: Under what condition does a convex lens form a virtual image, and what kind of image does a concave lens always form?
qa.a: A convex lens forms a virtual, erect and magnified image when the object is placed between the optical centre O and the principal focus F. A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image on the same side as the object between O and F.

qa.q: State the three standard rays used to draw ray diagrams for a convex lens.
qa.a: (1) A ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the principal focus F after refraction. (2) A ray passing through F emerges parallel to the principal axis. (3) A ray passing through the optical centre O goes straight without deviation.
qa.section: 9.3.5 Representation of Image Formation in Lenses Using Ray Diagrams

qa.q: What is the sign of the focal length f for a convex lens and for a concave lens?
qa.a: All distances are measured from the optical centre O. A convex lens has a positive focal length (f > 0), whereas a concave lens has a negative focal length (f < 0).

qa.q: Write the lens formula and magnification formula for a spherical lens.
qa.a: Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u. Magnification: m = h_i / h_o = v / u.

qa.q: Define the power of a lens, state its SI unit, and find the power of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm.
qa.a: The power of a lens (P) is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres: P = 1/f. Its SI unit is dioptre (1 D = 1 m⁻¹). For f = 20 cm = 0.20 m, P = 1 / 0.20 = +5 D.
